title: Temperature changes in reactions
aim: To investigate how the temperature of a reaction mixture changes when different volumes of sodium hydroxide solution are added to a fixed volume of hydrochloric acid.
background: Chemical reactions transfer energy to or from the surroundings. In an exothermic reaction, energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the temperature of the reaction mixture rises. Neutralisation, combustion and most oxidation reactions are exothermic. In an endothermic reaction, energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature falls; examples are thermal decompositions and the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate.

In this practical hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide solution: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l). The more alkali that reacts, the more energy is released, so the temperature rises as more alkali is added, until all the acid has been neutralised.

After the neutralisation point there is no acid left to react. Adding more sodium hydroxide solution (at room temperature) does not release any more energy and only cools and dilutes the mixture, so the temperature starts to fall.

A polystyrene cup is used because polystyrene is a good thermal insulator, and a lid reduces energy transfer to the surroundings by evaporation and convection. The cup is stood in a beaker so it does not fall over. The same method can be used to measure temperature changes for other reactions, such as a metal or a carbonate with an acid, or a displacement reaction.
hypothesis: The temperature of the mixture will increase as more sodium hydroxide is added, reaching a maximum when the acid is exactly neutralised (when equal volumes of the equal-concentration solutions have been mixed), and will then decrease as excess alkali is added.

variables.independent: Volume of sodium hydroxide solution added (0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 and 40 cm³).
variables.dependent: Highest temperature of the mixture reached after each addition (°C).
control: Concentration of sodium hydroxide solution (2.0 mol/dm³)
Starting temperature of both solutions (room temperature)
Type of container (polystyrene cup with a lid)

equipment: Polystyrene cup and lid (with a hole for the thermometer)
250 cm³ glass beaker (to support the cup)
Thermometer (−10 to 110 °C, reading to 0.1 °C or a digital thermometer)
Two 10 cm³ or 50 cm³ measuring cylinders
Glass stirring rod (or stir with the thermometer carefully)
method: Stand a polystyrene cup inside a 250 cm³ beaker so that it is stable.
Use a measuring cylinder to measure 30 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and pour it into the polystyrene cup.
Put the lid on the cup and push the thermometer through the hole in the lid so that the bulb is in the acid. Record the starting temperature of the acid.
Use a different measuring cylinder to measure 5 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution.
Lift the lid slightly, add the 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution to the cup, replace the lid quickly and stir the mixture.
Watch the thermometer and record the highest temperature reached.
Add a further 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution, stir, and record the highest temperature again.
Continue adding 5 cm³ portions of sodium hydroxide solution, stirring and recording the highest temperature each time, until a total of 40 cm³ has been added.
Rinse out the cup and repeat the whole experiment to get a second set of results. Calculate the mean highest temperature for each volume.

Plot a graph of mean highest temperature (y-axis) against volume of sodium hydroxide added (x-axis). Draw two straight lines of best fit, one through the rising points and one through the falling points, and extend them until they cross.
Read off the maximum temperature and the volume of sodium hydroxide at which the lines cross. Calculate the maximum temperature rise.

safety.risk: Corrosive; can cause serious eye damage and skin burns.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection (goggles), wipe up spills immediately and wash any splashes off skin with plenty of water.
Wear eye protection and wash splashes off skin with water.

safety.risk: Spilling corrosive solutions over the bench and skin.
safety.precaution: Stand the cup in a glass beaker so it is stable, and add solutions carefully.

safety.risk: Breaks if used to stir too hard, causing cuts.
safety.precaution: Stir gently with a glass rod, or use a digital thermometer probe; report breakages and do not pick up broken glass by hand.

results.notes: Plot mean highest temperature against volume of NaOH added. Draw one line of best fit through the rising points (0 to 30 cm³) and another through the falling points (30 to 40 cm³). The lines cross at about 30 cm³ and 31.5 °C. Maximum temperature rise = 31.5 − 19.1 = 12.4 °C.

analysis: The temperature increased each time sodium hydroxide was added, up to 30 cm³. This shows that neutralisation is exothermic: energy is transferred from the reacting chemicals to the surroundings (the solution), so its temperature rises.

The highest temperature (31.5 °C) was reached when 30 cm³ of sodium hydroxide had been added. At this point all the acid had been neutralised. This makes sense because both solutions had the same concentration (2.0 mol/dm³), so equal volumes contain equal numbers of moles, and HCl and NaOH react in a 1 : 1 ratio.

After 30 cm³, the temperature fell. No more acid was left, so no more energy was released, and the extra cooler sodium hydroxide solution absorbed energy from the mixture and diluted it. Energy was also lost to the surroundings.
The rise became smaller with each 5 cm³ addition (3.5 °C, then 2.7 °C, then 2.1 °C, and so on) because the energy released was shared out through a larger and larger volume of solution.
The maximum temperature rise was 12.4 °C. The true value would be a little higher because some energy was lost to the surroundings through the cup and lid and when the lid was lifted.

errors.error: Energy is lost to the surroundings through the sides and top of the cup, so the temperature rise measured is lower than the true value.
errors.improvement: Use a lid, a double polystyrene cup, or add insulation (for example cotton wool) around the cup; keep the lid on except when adding solution.

errors.error: The highest temperature is missed because the reading changes quickly.
errors.improvement: Stir continuously and watch the thermometer, or use a digital temperature probe and data logger that records the maximum.

errors.error: Measuring cylinders have a low resolution, so the volumes added are not exact.
errors.improvement: Use a burette or a pipette to add the sodium hydroxide.

errors.error: The neutralisation point may lie between two of the volumes tested, so the true maximum temperature may be missed.
errors.improvement: Use smaller additions (for example 1 cm³) near 30 cm³, and find the maximum from where the two lines of best fit cross.

errors.error: Thermometer readings are difficult to read precisely.
errors.improvement: Use a digital thermometer reading to 0.1 °C and read liquid thermometers at eye level.

examTips: Explain the polystyrene cup and lid in terms of energy: polystyrene is a thermal insulator and the lid reduces energy transfer to the surroundings, so the temperature change is more accurate.
In an exothermic reaction the temperature of the surroundings (the solution) goes up; in an endothermic reaction it goes down. Do not say the reaction 'makes heat'.
To find the maximum temperature from a graph, draw two straight lines of best fit and extend them until they cross; do not just join the dots.
Explain why the temperature falls after neutralisation: no acid is left to react, and the added cooler solution absorbs energy and dilutes the mixture.
Temperature change = highest (or lowest) temperature − starting temperature. Include the sign or say 'rise' or 'fall'.

options: Polystyrene does not react with acids
Polystyrene is a good thermal insulator, so less energy is transferred to the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: polystyrene is a (good thermal) insulator / reduces energy transfer to the surroundings
questions.explanation: Glass conducts energy away more easily than polystyrene. Reducing energy losses makes the measured temperature change closer to the true value.

questions.question: The temperature of the mixture rose when sodium hydroxide was added to hydrochloric acid. What type of reaction is this?
markScheme: 1 mark: exothermic
questions.explanation: An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises. In an endothermic reaction the temperature falls.

questions.question:
A student added sodium hydroxide solution to hydrochloric acid.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the maximum temperature rise.
questions.explanation: Temperature change = highest temperature − starting temperature. Adding the temperatures together is a common mistake.

questions.question: Give one reason why a lid is placed on the polystyrene cup.
markScheme: 1 mark: to reduce energy (heat) transfer to the surroundings / reduce energy lost by evaporation or convection
questions.explanation: Warm air and water vapour escaping from the top of the cup carry energy away, which would lower the temperature reading.

questions.question:
A student added different volumes of sodium hydroxide solution to hydrochloric acid and recorded the highest temperature reached.
The student did each experiment twice.
Table 1 shows some of the results.
Calculate the mean highest temperature, X, for 25 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution.

headers: Volume of sodium hydroxide solution in cm³

questions.explanation: Add the readings and divide by the number of readings. Give the mean to the same number of decimal places as the data (1 d.p.).

questions.question:
A student adds 2.0 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution, 5 cm³ at a time, to 30 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.
At which volume of sodium hydroxide solution would you expect the highest temperature?
markScheme: 1 mark: 30 cm³
questions.explanation: The solutions have the same concentration and react in a 1 : 1 ratio, so 30 cm³ of alkali exactly neutralises 30 cm³ of acid. This is where the most energy has been released.

markScheme: 1 mark: all the acid had been neutralised / no acid left to react, so no more energy is released
1 mark: the extra (cooler) sodium hydroxide solution absorbs energy / dilutes the mixture / energy is lost to the surroundings
questions.explanation: The reaction stops releasing energy once the acid is used up. The sodium hydroxide being added is at room temperature, so it cools the warmer mixture.

questions.question:
A student investigates how the volume of sodium hydroxide solution added to hydrochloric acid affects the temperature of the mixture.
Give two control variables in this investigation.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 2: volume of hydrochloric acid; concentration of hydrochloric acid; concentration of sodium hydroxide; starting temperature of solutions; type of container / insulation / lid; stirring
questions.explanation: The volume of sodium hydroxide is the independent variable, so it cannot be a control variable.

questions.question:
A student measures the temperature rise when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution in a polystyrene cup.
Which change would make the measured temperature rise closer to the true value?
options: Using a glass beaker instead of a polystyrene cup
Removing the lid so the thermometer is easier to read
Using a larger volume of more dilute acid
Placing the polystyrene cup inside a second polystyrene cup
markScheme: 1 mark: placing the cup inside a second polystyrene cup (more insulation)
questions.explanation: Extra insulation reduces energy transfer to the surroundings. A glass beaker or no lid would increase losses, and dilute acid would give a smaller temperature rise.

questions.question:
A student added 1.0 g of citric acid to sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
State the type of reaction and explain how the results show this.
markScheme: 1 mark: endothermic
1 mark: the temperature fell (by 4.3 °C), so energy was taken in from the surroundings
questions.explanation: In an endothermic reaction the reacting chemicals take in energy from the surroundings (the solution), so the thermometer shows a lower temperature.

questions.question:
A student added magnesium ribbon to hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup. The temperature changed from 20.5 °C to 38.0 °C.
Calculate the temperature change.
questions.explanation: Final temperature − initial temperature = 17.5 °C. The positive value shows a temperature rise, so the reaction is exothermic.

neutralisation point may fall between volumes tested
markScheme: 1 mark: the exact neutralisation point may lie between two of the volumes tested (so the highest reading may not be the true maximum)
1 mark: extrapolating the two lines to where they cross gives the true maximum temperature and volume / uses all the data so reduces the effect of random errors
questions.explanation: Readings were only taken every 5 cm³. The two lines represent before and after neutralisation, so they meet at the point where the acid was exactly neutralised.

questions.question:
A student adds 4.0 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution, 5 cm³ at a time, to 30 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid.
At which volume of sodium hydroxide solution would the highest temperature occur?
markScheme: 1 mark: 15 cm³
questions.explanation: 30 cm³ of 2.0 mol/dm³ HCl contains 0.060 mol. 4.0 mol/dm³ NaOH contains 0.060 mol in 0.060 ÷ 4.0 = 0.015 dm³ = 15 cm³. Doubling the alkali concentration halves the volume needed.

questions.question:
A student added sodium hydroxide solution, 5 cm³ at a time, to hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup.
Table 1 shows the first four results.
The temperature rise for each 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution got smaller as more was added.
Suggest why.

headers: Volume of sodium hydroxide solution added in cm³

acceptedAnswers: more energy lost as temperature difference increases
markScheme: 1 mark: each 5 cm³ releases the same amount of energy, but it is spread through a larger total volume (mass) of solution
1 mark: so the temperature rise is smaller / more energy is lost to the surroundings as the mixture gets hotter
questions.explanation: The same energy heating a bigger volume of liquid gives a smaller temperature rise. Also, the hotter the mixture is compared with the room, the faster it loses energy.

questions.question:
Describe a method to investigate how the volume of sodium hydroxide solution added to 30 cm³ of hydrochloric acid affects the temperature of the mixture.
Include how you would make the results as accurate as possible.
markScheme: Indicative content: measure 30 cm³ of hydrochloric acid with a measuring cylinder into a polystyrene cup; stand the cup in a beaker; put on a lid; insert thermometer and record starting temperature; add 5 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution (measured with measuring cylinder); stir; record highest temperature; repeat additions of 5 cm³ up to 40 cm³; control concentrations and volume of acid; repeat the experiment and calculate means; plot temperature against volume; draw two lines of best fit and find where they cross; accuracy: lid and polystyrene cup reduce energy losses, use burette for volumes, digital thermometer, stir to mix evenly

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method with measured volumes, recording of the highest temperature after each addition, repeats, and at least two ways of improving accuracy explained.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most of the steps, with some reference to reducing energy losses, but some detail missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as mix acid and alkali and measure the temperature, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The best answers include fixed and changing volumes, how temperature is measured, how energy losses are reduced, repeats, and how the data are processed to find the maximum.
